title: Sterling Ranch Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Sterling Ranch wells have a 105 ft median depth, but the range is wide. See yields, water levels, permits, risks and drilling costs.
h1: Sterling Ranch, Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Sterling Ranch show a wide range of conditions. Among 3,402 Colorado DWR permits, 2,197 report total depth and 672 report pump yield, so the depth and production statistics are useful but do not describe every permit.

The local median well is 105 feet deep, with a middle half from 40 to 440 feet. A completed well commonly produces around 12 gallons per minute, but a buyer should still review nearby well logs, the intended use, and the exact lot before relying on these area summaries.

sections.heading: Sterling Ranch well depths vary sharply across the area
sections.html:
The median reported depth near Sterling Ranch is 105 feet, but that number hides substantial variation. The middle half of wells runs from 40 to 440 feet. Nearly half, 48%, are under 100 feet, while 21% fall between 300 and 600 feet and 15% are deeper than 600 feet.

The deepest recorded well reaches 2,668 feet. That does not mean a new well will need to approach that depth. It does mean a driller should price the job from local logs and the target aquifer, not from the median alone. Permits name the Denver Basin on 62% of wells, with other records identifying fractured bedrock, Denver, or Arapahoe aquifers.

sections.heading: What Sterling Ranch wells produce
sections.html:
Reported pump yields are generally favorable. The median is 12.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. The largest group, 64%, produces between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 33% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Only 2% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and none are recorded under 1 gallon per minute. That is encouraging for household planning, but production is not the same as storage or water quality. Ask for the well-construction report, pumping test, casing and grout details, and any restrictions tied to the permit.

sections.heading: Water levels show a lower recorded depth in newer decades
sections.html:
The overall median static water level is 180 feet below the surface, with the middle half ranging from 22 to 328 feet. Measurements by decade show 209 feet in the 1980s, 44 feet in the 2010s, and 38 feet in the 2020s.

That series does not suggest a dropping water table in the recorded measurements; the reported depth to water is shallower in the newer decades. Treat the comparison carefully because the wells and measurement locations may differ. Before buying, have a professional confirm the static level at the property and check whether the well can meet the planned household, stock, or irrigation use.

sections.heading: Sterling Ranch permit history and local drillers
sections.html:
Permit activity was strongest in the 1990s, with 926 permits, followed by 692 in the 1980s and 580 in the 2000s. Records include 353 permits from the 2010s and 65 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025, so this is not an area with only historic well construction.

Among the most active names in the records are Hier Drilling Co Inc, also listed as Hier, Bruce A., with 507 records; Authorized, listed as Pe, Pg, with 310; and Arrow Drilling Co., listed as Berglund, Paul R., with 227. Confirm current licensing, availability, and scope directly before hiring.

sections.heading: A Sterling Ranch well may cost more than the median-depth estimate
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 105-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $5,200 to $7,400. That is only the drilling portion, not a ready-to-use water system.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $11,200 to $19,400 at the median depth. A lot requiring a deeper hole can exceed that range. Get a written bid that separates drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, waterline trenching, electrical work, testing, and permit-related work. The wide local depth range makes allowances especially important.

sections.heading: Environmental and construction checks before you commit
sections.html:
Nearby well production looks solid overall, but a buyer still needs property-specific checks. Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 70 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 17 historic mine features, and 9 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those records do not prove a particular parcel is contaminated, but they justify water testing and a review of local site history.

Also confirm separation from septic components, the proposed building location, access for a drill rig, and room for the pressure tank and treatment equipment. A permitted domestic well is not automatically suitable for every proposed use. If production is poor or a hole is dry, the cost and permitting consequences can be substantial.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Louviers and Roxborough Park
sections.html:
Use the nearby records as a starting point, then narrow the comparison to wells close to the parcel. Louviers and Roxborough Park are each about 3 miles away, while Highlands Ranch is about 5 miles away. Sedalia, Columbine, and Ken Caryl provide additional regional context, but geology and aquifer conditions can change across short distances.

Before closing, obtain the DWR permit and construction report, verify the permitted use, ask for recent water-quality and production information, and have a driller review neighboring depths. For a new build, coordinate the well, driveway, septic system, utility trenching, and house site before excavation. In an over-appropriated basin, confirm whether an augmentation plan or other water-rights requirement applies.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Sterling Ranch?
faq.a: The median reported depth near Sterling Ranch is 105 feet. The middle half ranges from 40 to 440 feet, so nearby properties can differ substantially. 48% of reported wells are under 100 feet, while 15% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 2,668 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Sterling Ranch?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 105-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $5,200 to $7,400. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $11,200 to $19,400. Deeper-than-median wells can cost more.

faq.q: How much water do Sterling Ranch wells produce?
faq.a: Reported wells have a median pump yield of 12.0 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. 64% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 33% exceed 15 gallons per minute. Confirm the individual well's pumping test before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Sterling Ranch?
faq.a: The area records include 70 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, along with historic mine and cleanup sites. That does not establish contamination at a specific home. Test the property well for relevant contaminants, review nearby land uses, and retest after construction or changes to the water system.

faq.q: Are Sterling Ranch wells getting deeper or losing water?
faq.a: The recorded static water levels do not show a simple decline. Median depth to water was 209 feet in the 1980s, 44 feet in the 2010s, and 38 feet in the 2020s. Because the measurements may come from different wells and locations, verify the current static level and production at the property.
